Zice Sun Datasheet as part of GripRx for Team 103

Submission: Sep 1st, 2026

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet documents my individual contributions to the Team 103 design project for EGR 304, Fall 2026.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: Team 103 is designing GripRx, a prescription-based automatic-resistance grip trainer for hand rehabilitation. The device measures the force a patient applies through a load cell and automatically sets its own mechanical resistance to the level prescribed by a therapist. The system is split into three boards, each built around a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano: a UI board, a force sensing board, and a motor board, connected in a daisy chain by 8-pin ribbon cables.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text: I design the force sensing board, the center board of the daisy chain. It measures grip force (load cell, INA125P instrumentation amplifier and active low-pass filter into the ADC), runs the training-session logic, and exchanges messages with the UI board and the motor board.

docs.title: Block Diagram: Force Sensing Board
docs.text: Zice Sun · Team 103 (Duotao Gao, Gabriel Toneser Facchin, Zice Sun) · Project: GripRx, a prescription-based automatic-resistance grip trainer

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page shows the hardware layout of my subsystem, the force sensing board, and how it connects to my teammates' boards. The block diagram is the starting point for component selection and the schematic: it fixes which microcontroller peripherals and pins I use, which signals cross the ribbon cables, and which power rail each part runs on.

  • Role in the system. The force sensing board sits in the middle of the team's daisy chain. It measures grip force, runs the training-session logic, and talks to the UI board (Duotao Gao) on ribbon connector J1 and to the motor board (Gabriel Toneser Facchin) on ribbon connector J2.
  • Sensor. A Phidgets 3135_0 50 kg load cell (Wheatstone bridge) produces a millivolt-level differential signal. It is amplified by a Texas Instruments INA125P instrumentation amplifier and smoothed by an active low-pass filter built on a Microchip MCP6004 op amp before it reaches the ADC on pin RA0. Each signal-conditioning stage is a separate block.
  • Outputs to teammates. The board has no actuator of its own. It sends a FORCE_OK safety line (digital output RD1) and an analog copy of the force (FORCE_ANA, DAC output RA2) to the motor board, and exchanges UART messages with both boards.
  • Power. A 9 V, 3 A wall adapter (BestCH, issued in class) feeds an STMicroelectronics L7805ABV-DG linear regulator, which supplies a regulated 5 V rail to every part on the board. No power is passed over the ribbon cables; pin 8 of each ribbon only shares ground.

docs.title: Component Selection: Force Sensing Board
docs.text: Zice Sun · Team 103 (Duotao Gao, Gabriel Toneser Facchin, Zice Sun) · Project: GripRx, a prescription-based automatic-resistance grip trainer

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page compares at least three candidate solutions for every major component of my subsystem, the force sensing board, and explains which one I chose and why. The components follow the blocks of my individual block diagram: the load cell, the instrumentation amplifier, the op amp for the active low-pass filter, the 5 V voltage regulator and the 9 V external power source. The microcontroller (PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano) is not compared because it was selected for the class.

All five components belong to my individual subsystem and are labeled in bold as [Individual subsystem: force sensing board]. The board has no actuator or other electro-mechanical part of its own; the motor and lead screw are on Gabriel's motor board.

The selections were judged against these project specifications and course constraints:

  • Measure grip force from 0 to 40 kgf with 0.1 kgf resolution on the PIC's 12-bit ADC (0 to 5 V).
  • Run every part from one regulated +5 V rail, fed by a 9 V wall adapter through a through-hole linear regulator.
  • Use bare components only (no breakout or daughter boards) in packages the Peralta mill can make (pin pitch ≥ 0.8 mm), so DIP, SOIC, TO-92 and TO-220 are acceptable but MSOP and QFN are not.
  • Include an op amp stage in the sensor signal chain; any other amplifier needs instructor approval.
  • Stay within the $60 individual budget; parts handed out in class do not count against it.

Prices are for quantity 1, checked on 2026-10-16 at the linked vendor unless noted.

docs.title: 1. Force Sensor (Load Cell)
docs.text:
Table 1: Load cell selection

Load cell — [Individual subsystem: force sensing board]

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Phidgets 3135_0 (CZL635-50) 50 kg straight-bar load cell$7.00/eachPhidgets 3135_0 product page * Full 4-wire Wheatstone bridge connects straight to the instrumentation amplifier inputs* 50 kg capacity covers the 40 kgf maximum grip with 25 % headroom* Rated output 1 mV/V and a published spec sheet (repeatability, creep, zero balance, 5 V maximum excitation)* Aluminum bar with M5 threaded holes is easy to mount inside the grip handle* Inexpensive, with 239 in stock * Small output: only 5 mV at full scale with 5 V excitation, so it needs a gain of about 750* Sold by Phidgets, not Digi-Key, so it adds a second order and shipping charge* Zero balance and temperature drift must be removed by taring in firmware Option 2.SparkFun SEN-10245 50 kg load sensor (bathroom-scale corner cell)$6.25/each (Digi-Key, 2026-10-04)SparkFun SEN-10245 at Digi-Key * Lowest unit price of the three options* Available from Digi-Key, so it can share one order with the rest of the board* Same 1 mV/V class of output as Option 1 * Half bridge (3 wires): needs a second cell or two precision completion resistors to form a full bridge* Completion resistors add temperature drift that a full bridge cancels* Flat bathroom-scale shape is designed to sit under a platform and is hard to fit into a hand grip Option 3.Interlink FSR 402 force sensitive resistor (SparkFun SEN-09375)$10.95/each (Mouser)SparkFun SEN-09375 at Mouser * Very thin and light, can be glued onto the grip surface* Large resistance change: a simple voltage divider and op amp buffer can read it without an instrumentation amplifier* Responds to light touches, useful for detecting that the user is holding the grip * Saturates at a few kilograms, far below the 40 kgf grip range* Strongly nonlinear, with drift and part-to-part variation of several percent, so it cannot meet the 0.1 kgf resolution goal* Most expensive of the three for the worst measurement accuracy

Choice: Option 1: Phidgets 3135_0 50 kg straight-bar load cell.

Rationale: GripRx sets the motor resistance from the measured grip force, so the force reading must be accurate and repeatable across the whole 0–40 kgf range. Only the two strain-gauge cells can measure that range; the force sensitive resistor saturates at a few kilograms and is too nonlinear for a therapy prescription. Between the two load cells, the Phidgets cell is a complete full bridge, which cancels temperature effects and wires directly to the INA125P with no completion resistors, and its straight-bar shape bolts into the handle. At 5 V excitation it gives 0.1 mV per kgf, so 40 kgf produces 4 mV; with a total gain of about 750 this becomes about 3 V at the ADC, and 0.1 kgf is about 6 ADC counts, which meets the resolution goal. The separate Phidgets order is the main drawback; if the shipping pushes me over budget I will buy the cell out of pocket, which the course allows.

docs.title: 2. Instrumentation Amplifier
docs.text:
Table 2: Instrumentation amplifier selection

Instrumentation amplifier — [Individual subsystem: force sensing board]

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Texas Instruments INA125P instrumentation amplifier (DIP-16)$12.78/each (Mouser)TI INA125P at Mouser * Designed for bridge sensors: high CMRR (100 dB minimum at G = 100 to 500) rejects the 2.5 V common-mode level of the bridge* Gain set by one resistor, G = 4 + 60 kΩ/RG, from 4 to 10,000* Low offset (250 µV maximum) and low quiescent current (525 µA maximum)* Runs from a single 2.7 V to 36 V supply, so it works on the 5 V rail* DIP package plugs straight into a breadboard for prototyping * Most expensive of the three options* On a single 5 V supply the output only swings from about 1 V to 3.3 V (worst case), so the REF pin must be offset and part of the gain is moved into the filter stage* Not an op amp, so it needs instructor approval Option 2.Microchip MCP6N11-100E/SN instrumentation amplifier (SOIC-8)$1.77/each (Mouser)Microchip MCP6N11-100E/SN at Mouser * Rail-to-rail input and output on a single 1.8 V to 5.5 V supply, so the whole 0–5 V ADC range is usable* Inexpensive and in the SOIC-8 package the mill can make* The "-100" version is stable at high gain, which suits the gain of about 750 this board needs* Gain set by two resistors * Higher input offset than the INA125P, which must be removed by taring* 5.5 V maximum supply leaves little margin above the 5 V rail* SOIC needs an adapter board for breadboard testing* Only 5 in stock at Mouser today (more expected 10/19); also needs instructor approval Option 3 (custom).Three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier built from 2× Microchip MCP6V27-E/SN zero-drift dual op amps and 0.1 % resistors$3.20/each, $6.40 for two (Mouser)Microchip MCP6V27-E/SN at Mouser * Built only from op amps, so it satisfies the "op amp stage" rule without special approval* Zero-drift op amps have about ±2 µV offset, far below the 10 µV per 0.1 kgf signal step* Rail-to-rail input and output on the 5 V rail* The fourth op amp is free to buffer the reference voltage * CMRR depends on resistor matching: about 7 precision resistors must be matched to 0.1 %* More parts, more board area and more layout and soldering work* Two SOIC-8 packages need adapters for breadboard testing

Choice: Option 1: Texas Instruments INA125P (pending instructor approval; Option 3 is the fallback).

Rationale: The load cell signal is only 4 mV at 40 kgf riding on a 2.5 V common-mode voltage, so the first stage must reject common-mode voltage very well while adding almost no offset. The INA125P is a single, proven bridge amplifier: one resistor sets the gain (RG ≈ 80 Ω gives about 750), its CMRR is guaranteed, and it comes in a DIP package so I can prove the whole chain on a breadboard before the PCB is milled. Its limited output swing on a 5 V supply is handled by biasing the REF pin with a buffered voltage from the MCP6004 and taking part of the gain in the filter stage. The MCP6N11 is the lowest-cost option, but its offset is higher and its stock is low. If the INA125P is not approved, I will build Option 3, which needs no approval because it is made only of op amps, at the cost of more parts and resistor matching.

docs.title: 3. Op Amp for the Active Low-Pass Filter
docs.text:
Table 3: Low-pass filter op amp selection

Low-pass filter op amp — [Individual subsystem: force sensing board]

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Microchip MCP6004-I/P quad op amp (DIP-14)$0.60/each (Mouser); issued in class, $0 to my budgetMicrochip MCP6004-I/P at Mouser * Already in my class kit, so it costs nothing and is available now* Four op amps in one package: Sallen-Key filter, REF buffer and a spare for a gain stage* Rail-to-rail input and output on 1.8 V to 6.0 V, so it drives the ADC across nearly 0–5 V* 1 MHz gain-bandwidth is far above the 10 Hz cutoff* DIP package for breadboard prototyping * Offset up to ±4.5 mV, although after the INA125P gain this equals only about 6 µV at the input and is removed by taring* Larger package than a dual op amp* Lower precision than newer CMOS op amps Option 2.Microchip MCP6002-I/P dual op amp (DIP-8)$0.45/each (Mouser)Microchip MCP6002-I/P at Mouser * Same rail-to-rail, 1 MHz family as the MCP6004, so the filter design is identical* Smaller DIP-8 footprint* Inexpensive and widely stocked * Only two op amps: the filter and REF buffer use both, leaving no spare* Must be purchased, while the MCP6004 is already in hand Option 3.Texas Instruments TLV9062IDR dual op amp (SOIC-8)$1.05/each (Mouser)TI TLV9062IDR at Mouser * Lower offset (±0.3 mV typical) and 10 MHz gain-bandwidth* Rail-to-rail input and output on 1.8 V to 5.5 V* SOIC-8 is compact and millable * Surface-mount only, so it needs an adapter for breadboard testing* 5.5 V maximum supply leaves little margin above 5 V* Extra precision and speed are not needed for a 10 Hz filter after a high-gain stage

Choice: Option 1: Microchip MCP6004-I/P.

Rationale: The filter sits after the instrumentation amplifier, so the op amp's offset and noise are divided by the front-end gain of about 750 and no longer matter; what matters is rail-to-rail output into the ADC, enough op amps for the filter and the REF buffer, and an easy package. The MCP6004 meets all three, is already in my kit (so it costs nothing), and its four op amps cover the second-order Sallen-Key low-pass filter (cutoff about 10 Hz, well above the few hertz of a human grip and low enough to remove 60 Hz pickup), the REF buffer for the INA125P, and one spare. It also provides the op amp stage the course requires in the sensor signal chain.

docs.title: 4. 5 V Voltage Regulator
docs.text:
Table 4: 5 V regulator selection

+5 V linear regulator — [Individual subsystem: force sensing board]

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.STMicroelectronics L7805ABV-DG 5 V, 1.5 A linear regulator (TO-220)$1.04/each (Mouser); issued in class, $0 to my budgetST L7805ABV-DG at Mouser * 1.5 A output covers the worst-case 497 mA budget for the 5 V rail with large margin* ±2 % output tolerance (AB grade) and internal current limit and thermal shutdown* 7 V to 35 V input works with the 9 V adapter* Through-hole TO-220 is easy to solder and bolts to a heatsink* Already in my class kit and used by all three team boards * About 2 V dropout, so the input must stay above 7 V* Linear regulator wastes (9 V − 5 V) × I as heat: about 2 W at the worst-case budget, so it needs a heatsink* Higher quiescent current than a modern LDO Option 2.Texas Instruments LM2940CT-5.0/NOPB 5 V, 1 A low-dropout regulator (TO-220)$2.04/each (Mouser)TI LM2940CT-5.0/NOPB at Mouser * Low dropout (0.5 V typical at 1 A), so it keeps working if the input sags toward 6 V* 1 A output still covers the worst-case budget* Reverse-battery and mirror-insertion protection* Same TO-220 footprint as Option 1 * Out of stock at Mouser, with stock expected January 2027 (20-week lead time)* Needs a larger output capacitor with a controlled ESR to stay stable* Costs more and is not in the class kit Option 3.Microchip MCP1702-5002E/TO 5 V, 250 mA low-dropout regulator (TO-92)$0.65/each (Mouser)Microchip MCP1702-5002E/TO at Mouser * Very low quiescent current (about 2 µA), useful for battery designs* Small through-hole TO-92 package* Needs only two small ceramic capacitors * 250 mA maximum output is below the worst-case 497 mA budget for the 5 V rail* 13.2 V maximum input leaves little margin for adapter overshoot* TO-92 can only dissipate a fraction of a watt, so a 4 V drop limits it to about 100 mA in practice

Choice: Option 1: STMicroelectronics L7805ABV-DG.

Rationale: The power budget puts the worst-case 5 V rail current at 497 mA including the 25 % safety margin, which rules out the 250 mA MCP1702. Both TO-220 regulators can supply it, but the L7805ABV-DG is already in my kit, is the regulator the whole team uses (shared footprint and spares), and is in stock, while the LM2940 is back-ordered until 2027. Its 2 V dropout is not a problem because the 9 V adapter leaves 2 V of headroom above the 7 V minimum input. At the worst-case budget it would dissipate about 2 W, so I will mount it on a Boyd 507302B00000G TO-220 heatsink ($0.34); at the expected normal draw of under 100 mA it dissipates less than 0.4 W.

docs.title: 5. External Power Source (9 V Wall Adapter)
docs.text:
Table 5: External power source selection

9 V wall adapter — [Individual subsystem: force sensing board]

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.BestCH 9 V 3 A switching wall adapter (issued in class)$4.52/each (Amazon B09ZTKTLGW); $0 to my budgetBestCH 9 V 3 A adapter on Amazon * 3 A output covers the regulator's full 1.5 A rating with 1.5 A to spare* Already issued in class, so it costs nothing and is available now* 9 V gives the L7805 its required 2 V of headroom without excessive heat* 100–240 VAC input and a 5.5 mm barrel plug * No manufacturer datasheet, only the specifications in the store listing* Plug inner diameter and polarity are not stated, so the fit to the PJ-102AH jack and center-positive polarity must be checked with a multimeter before first power-up* Amazon parts are not reimbursable, so a replacement would come out of pocket Option 2.Triad Magnetics WSU090-2000 9 V 2 A wall adapter$12.43/each (Mouser)Triad WSU090-2000 at Mouser * Full datasheet: ±5 % regulation, 150 mV ripple maximum, short-circuit and over-voltage protection* UL 62368-1 listed and DoE Level VI efficient* 2.1 × 5.5 mm center-positive plug matches standard barrel jacks* 2 A covers the regulator's 1.5 A rating * Costs $12.43 of my budget plus shipping* Only 500 mA of spare capacity above the regulator rating* Must be ordered and waited for Option 3.Adafruit 63 9 V 1 A regulated switching wall adapter$8.95/each (Adafruit)Adafruit 63 product page * UL listed, with a datasheet linked on the product page* 2.1 × 5.5 mm center-positive plug* Small and light; 100–240 VAC input * 1 A is less than the regulator's 1.5 A rating, so the power budget's source check fails (−500 mA)* Adds another vendor, order and shipping charge* Costs more than the class-issued adapter

Choice: Option 1: BestCH 9 V 3 A wall adapter (class-issued), with Option 2 as the documented backup.

Rationale: The power budget requires the source to supply the full rating of every regulator connected to it. The BestCH adapter supplies 3 A against the L7805's 1.5 A, so 1.5 A remains, and it is already in hand at no cost. A 9 V supply is the best voltage for this board: it gives the L7805 its 2 V of dropout headroom while keeping the regulator's heat lower than a 12 V adapter would. Because the adapter has no manufacturer datasheet, I will measure its polarity and no-load voltage and check the plug fit on the PJ-102AH jack before connecting the board. If it fails those checks, the Triad WSU090-2000 is the replacement: it has a full datasheet and safety listing and still passes the power budget at 2 A. The Adafruit adapter was rejected because its 1 A rating fails the source check.

This schematic shows the GripRx force sensing board. docs.title: Power Budget: Force Sensing Board
docs.text: Zice Sun · Team 103 · Project: GripRx

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The power budget checks that the voltage regulator and the external power source I selected on the Component Selection page can power every part of the force sensing board at the same time, even in the worst case. It uses the class template and lists each major component's absolute maximum current from its datasheet, so the result is a safe upper bound rather than a typical value. The force sensing board has its own wall adapter and regulator, so it gets its own power budget, separate from my teammates' boards.

The design follows the walkthrough's advice to keep the number of power rails as small as possible: every part on this board runs from a single +5 V rail. The op amps and the instrumentation amplifier are single-supply parts, so no negative rail is needed, and nothing needs +12 V or +3.3 V. The unused rails in the template are marked "not used".

docs.title: Power Budget
docs.text: Figure 1: Power budget for the force sensing board, filled in on the class template.

docs.title: How Each Section Was Filled In
docs.text:
A. Major components. Four components draw power from the board; the regulator and power source are not listed here, as the template instructs. Each current is the absolute maximum from the datasheet:

Component Part number Supply range Absolute maximum current Datasheet basis PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano DM164150 1.8 – 5.5 V 350 mA Maximum current on the VDD pin, 40/44/48-pin devices, −40 °C to +85 °C Instrumentation amplifier INA125P 2.7 – 36 V 12.5 mA 0.525 mA maximum quiescent current plus 12 mA output short-circuit current Quad op amp MCP6004-I/P 1.8 – 6.0 V 30 mA Maximum current at the supply pins Load cell excitation Phidgets 3135_0 5 V maximum 5 mA 5 V across the 1 kΩ bridge

B. Power rails. All four components are on the +5 V rail. Their total is 397.5 mA; with the 25 % safety margin (which also covers the passive parts, the debug LED and other small loads) the rail must supply 496.9 mA.

C. Regulator. The STMicroelectronics L7805ABV-DG can supply 1500 mA, leaving 1003.1 mA of spare current on the +5 V rail. At the worst-case load it would dissipate (9 V − 5 V) × 0.497 A ≈ 2.0 W, so it gets a Boyd 507302B00000G TO-220 heatsink; the expected normal draw is under 100 mA (about 0.4 W). The regulator comparison (L7805ABV-DG, LM2940CT-5.0, MCP1702) is in Table 4 of the Component Selection page.

D. External power source. The class-issued BestCH 9 V 3 A wall adapter feeds the only regulator. Counting the regulator at its full 1500 mA rating, 1500 mA remains, so the adapter can supply the board in every case. A 9 V input gives the L7805ABV-DG its required 2 V of dropout headroom (7 V minimum input). The adapter comparison is in Table 5 of the Component Selection page.

E. Battery life. Not applicable: the board is powered from the wall and has no battery.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: The force sensing board needs only one regulated +5 V rail. In the worst case it needs 496.9 mA including the 25 % safety margin; the L7805ABV-DG regulator (1500 mA) and the 9 V 3 A adapter (3000 mA) both have positive remaining current, so the selected regulator and power source are sufficient. The main design consequence is heat: the regulator must have a heatsink so that it stays safe even at the worst-case current.
